items.title: China’s factories are growing profits again, but the AI boom is picking the winners
items.summary: China's economy has been running at two speeds, with AI-related manufacturing and exports powering growth while consumption, real estate investment lag.
items.body: China's industrial profits in October grew at their fastest pace since May, supported by an AI-driven electronics boom and higher energy prices, while consumer-facing industries squeezed by weak demand continued to be a drag. Profits at sizeable industrial firms surged 20.1% in October from a year earlier, according to data released Friday by the National Bureau of Statistics. For the first 10 months this year, the earnings grew 16% year on year, having risen 15.5% through September. That extends a notable rebound in 2026 after three years of declines followed by a tepid 0.6% growth last year, with profits on track to log their strongest annual expansion since 2021.

items.title: Labour row over Rosebank deepens as dozens of MPs warn PM not to block oilfield
items.summary: Warning of ‘lights out for Labour in Scotland’ as Burnham faces choice between warring factions over North Sea drilling project Dozens of Labour MPs in favour of Rosebank are putting pressure on the prime minister not to block the North Sea oilfield, warning that doing so could…
items.body: Dozens of Labour MPs in favour of Rosebank are putting pressure on the prime minister not to block the North Sea oilfield, warning that doing so could spell “lights out for Labour in Scotland”. As many as 80 pro-drilling MPs are considering writing their own letter to Andy Burnham after nearly 100 of their colleagues called on the prime minister not to allow the project to proceed . Scottish Labour leader Michael Marra has also reiterated his support for Rosebank, cautioning that “working-class people in vocational jobs” were threatened by the decline of the North Sea basin. Burnham now faces having to choose between two warring factions within his own party in what is likely to be the most sensitive decision he has taken so far as prime minister. Anti-Rosebank MPs warn about the impact on the climate.

items.title: Airline Norse Atlantic files for bankruptcy, succumbing to aviation fuel costs
items.summary: The low-cost airline was only founded a few years ago and had been struggling to turn a profit. The spike in aviation fuel prices caused by the war in Iran has now driven Norway's Norse Atlantic into bankruptcy.
items.body: Norwegian low-cost, long-haul airline Norse Atlantic's operating unit has declared bankruptcy, the carrier said on Friday. The airline had warned on Wednesday that its financial situation was "critical," and suspended all flights the following day, saying it was urgently seeking emergency funding to fend off bankruptcy. Like many commercial airlines, Norse Atlantic is highly exposed to the vastly increased jet fuel prices of 2026, attributable in very large part to the war in Iran and resultant tension throughout the wider Middle East. Norse had said slightly earlier on Friday that its lessors had terminated their leasing contracts for all 12 aircraft in the carrier's fleet, demanding that the planes be handed back. Initially the company said it planned to contest this claim, which would have rendered it effectively unable to operate.

items.title: Spain’s election could pull Madrid closer to Trump’s Washington
items.summary: Spanish voters head to the polls on Sunday for a snap election that could bring socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's eight years in power to an end.
items.body: Spanish voters head to the polls on Sunday for a snap election that could bring down socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, who has repeatedly clashed with U.S. President Donald Trump. It could also put the far right in government for the first time in the country's modern democratic era. The center-right Popular Party is the frontrunner, and it could win a majority with far-right Vox, according to El País ' s final polling averages . A government led by the PP could shift Spain's approach to Washington, Beijing and NATO. It's the first test of whether Europe's mainstream conservatives are willing to bring the far right into government, ahead of elections in France and Poland next year. Despite Spain's economy growing 2.7% year over year in the third quarter, more than twice the euro zone's 1.3%, the campaign has been dominated by housing and cost-of-living crises.

items.title: From £250 job to £9,000 bill: Inside the rogue trader networks scamming customers at scale
items.summary: Networks of plumbers and electricians are scamming people on a large scale, the BBC reveals.
items.body: Organised networks of rogue plumbers and electricians have been scamming people on a large scale, a BBC investigation has found. Nessar Khawaja, who used the online name ThatGuyNess, regularly posted TikTok videos showing his work as a plumber, explaining how he made thousands of pounds from "desperate" customers, and recruiting online to expand his network. The investigation found the 23-year-old is a key figure within an organised group that is systematically ripping off customers and teaching others to do the same. The BBC put these allegations to Khawaja in writing. He denied any wrongdoing and said his social media posts were intended as light-hearted comedy that did not reflect how he operated in practice. In a recorded phone call, Khawaja insisted he was an entertainer, was joking and that the BBC had "taken things out of context".

items.title: Norse Atlantic Airways files for bankruptcy and cancels all future flights
items.summary: Norwegian airline tells customers not to come to airports after surging fuel costs caused by Iran war ruin finances Norse Atlantic Airways has filed for bankruptcy and cancelled all future flights after surging fuel costs caused by the Iran war ruined its finances. The Norwegian…
items.body: Norse Atlantic Airways has filed for bankruptcy and cancelled all future flights after surging fuel costs caused by the Iran war ruined its finances. The Norwegian airline said it was entering insolvency and posted a message on its website telling customers not to come to airports – including passengers stranded away from home. Its collapse came a day after it put flights on hold with a warning that its finances were critical. The carrier operated low-cost, long-haul flights around the world, including from London Gatwick and the US to Europe and Asia. Flights from Gatwick and Manchester next month to Thailand are among those now scrapped, along with London flights to South Africa and the US.

items.title: Indian workers fill Germany's labor gaps but face hurdles and risks
items.summary: The number of Indians working in Germany has grown rapidly in recent years. But many continue to face challenges in the labor market. Some also fall victim to recruitment scams, leaving them vulnerable to exploitation.
items.body: Pratyay Saikia was studying food technology in 2022 when he saw an advertisement from Magic Billion, a recruitment agency that places skilled and semi-skilled Indian professionals in verified jobs abroad. The 25-year-old from the northern Indian state of Haryana reached out to explore employment opportunities. Four years later, he is working as a butcher at Metzgerei Lederer in southern Germany , having completed a three-year apprenticeship at the butcher shop. "I came to Baden-Württemberg with 180 other Indians who came here to do an Ausbildung [apprenticeship] program. Me and seven others did our Ausbildung at Lederer [butcher shop], while others went into the construction sector. I now have a full-time job here," Saikia told DW.

items.title: ECB Consumer Expectations Survey results – October 2026
items.body: In October the median rate of perceived inflation over the previous 12 months increased to 4.1% from 3.6% in September and stood at its highest level since July 2024. Median expectations for inflation over the next 12 months also rose to 3.5% from 3.1%, but remained below the level reached at the start of the conflict in March 2026 (4.0%). Median expectations for inflation three years ahead increased to 3.0% from 2.9%, returning to the March 2026 level. Median expectations for inflation five years ahead were unchanged at 2.5% for the third consecutive month, the highest level since the start of the series in August 2022. Uncertainty about expectations for inflation over the next 12 months increased for the second consecutive month, remaining higher than the level prior to the start of the conflict in the Middle East.

items.summary: Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi said "The incident is suspicious and looks like a precooked recipe for war."
items.body: Two Italians have been killed after an alleged Iranian attack on Kuwait, Kuwaiti forces said Thursday. In a post on X , Kuwait's army said the deaths followed Iranian attacks on the country, with the two Italians killed by falling missile debris. Two others were also injured. In response, a spokesperson for Iran's military told state media that no offensive or military operations had been carried out in the area and that "these accusations should be viewed as a cover for continued malevolence and an attempt to exacerbate insecurity in the region" by U.S. and Israeli forces. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Telegram that he had spoken with his Italian counterpart, Antonio Tajani, and expressed regret over their deaths, while stressing that Tehran had no role or involvement in the incident.

items.title: Even the price of toys is on the rise. How Americans are scaling back holiday plans
items.summary: U.S. consumers face higher food, travel and gift costs in 2026 as inflation and Iran-war energy shocks pressure holiday budgets.
items.body: As Amanda Brecht planned how her family would spend Thanksgiving this year, she had to make some difficult decisions. Because of high gas prices , the 30-year-old decided she wouldn't drive across her home state of Michigan to celebrate with extended family. Instead, Brecht and her husband will spend the holiday with just their three kids. And with food prices rising, they'll be skipping appetizers and serving turkey breast instead of a whole bird. "Thanksgiving is definitely going to look different this year," Brecht said. "Money doesn't grow on trees. You can only do so much." With inflation accelerating, Americans like Brecht will see higher prices almost everywhere they look this holiday season . At a time of year synonymous with food, gifts and big spending, many consumers are instead pinching pennies, paring back their plans and making tough choices about how they'll celebrate.

items.title: UK to pay 'participation' fee to deliver EU deals
items.summary: Details of the contribution towards EU running costs have been revealed in new legal documents.
items.body: The UK will pay a "participation fee" to the EU as part of the deals agreed by Andy Burnham, according to legal documents. The surcharge will go towards the running costs of EU agencies and systems required to deliver two of the agreements unveiled by the prime minister last week. It will be paid in addition to a contribution towards costs that broadly mirrors how EU members contribute to the bloc's shared budget, the documents show. The government has sought to contrast the financial costs of the deals against their overall effect on the economy, which it estimates will receive an eventual boost by billions a year due to increased trade. The government is yet to publish an estimate of overall additional costs, but officials said they expected them to be in the low tens of millions per year and "massively outweighed" by predicted economic gains.

items.title: British Gas owner seeks urgent government talks over future of storage facility
items.summary: Centrica boss memo to 400 workers at gas plant off Yorkshire coast says utility doing all it can ‘to save your jobs’ The boss of the British Gas owner Centrica has told hundreds of staff at its largest gas storage facility that he was seeking urgent talks with Andy Burnham and…
items.body: The boss of the British Gas owner Centrica has told hundreds of staff at its largest gas storage facility that he was seeking urgent talks with Andy Burnham and would do everything he could to save jobs. Chris O’Shea, the chief executive of Centrica, reportedly told staff at the Rough gas storage facility off the east Yorkshire that the government had rebuffed the company’s plea for short-term support to run the store over the winter. In a memo, seen by Sky News, O’Shea is understood to have expressed disappointment that the government had delayed its response to a consultation on whether to support the ageing underground gas stores over the longer term. The Guardian understands that the government delivered its decision to Centrica in the last few weeks and the internal company memo was intended to update the facility’s staff about continuing talks.

items.summary: Budget carrier Norse Atlantic filed for bankruptcy Friday, saying it failed to secure funding after soaring fuel costs strained the company's operations.
items.body: Budget carrier Norse Atlantic filed for bankruptcy Friday, saying it failed to secure funding after soaring fuel costs strained the company's operations throughout the year. Its parent company, Norse Atlantic ASA, concluded that the Norwegian carrier no longer has a basis to continue operations. "Despite extensive efforts, the Company has so far not been able to secure sufficient funding to meet its short-term liquidity needs," the firm said in a statement Friday. It comes days after Norse said it's facing a "critical financial situation" and was considering its options from a strategic takeover to ACMI contracts, which refer to short-term capacity leasing. The company's shares closed 85% lower on Wednesday. The board has now filed a bankruptcy petition with the Agder District Court, where a trustee will be appointed to manage the process further.

Those jolts were felt particularly in Asia as the saga highlighted the region's huge exposure to the technology. Tech-heavy stock indexes in Japan, South Korea and Taiwan went on a rollercoaster ride this week. Markets soared after a near-trillion dollar surge in Nvidia's share price but then slumped as concerns about political and regulatory scrutiny hit investor confidence. The chipmaker is a "symbolic bellwether" of the AI trade that is fast becoming key to places like South Korea, Taiwan, Singapore and Malaysia," says Dylan Loh, an international studies lecturer at Nanyang Technological University.

items.body: Poundland staff fear they’ll be left out in the cold for Christmas. When will workers have a say in their future? “I feel Gordon Brothers punched us in the guts and took us down,” says Kelvin Blake, one of thousands of Poundland workers at risk of redundancy after the budget retailer’s US-based owners rejected at least two solvent bids for it. While administrators at AlixPartners, who were appointed on Wednesday, continue to consider bids for the whole group, which has 600 stores in the UK and Ireland including the Dealz chain, more than 10,000 staff and thousands of suppliers face a grim Christmas of uncertainty. The impact is being felt at Poundland stores across the country, as well at its head office and its distribution centres, including one in Andy Burnham’s Makerfield constituency.

items.title: EU leaders fail to break $1.7 trillion budget deadlock as political pressure mounts
items.summary: EU leaders failed to break a deadlock over the bloc’s budget, with talks set to resume in December as a key deadline looms.
items.body: European leaders failed to break a deadlock over the EU's next long-term budget on Thursday, leaving negotiators under pressure to meet their year-end target before a busy 2027 election cycle adds further complications. National leaders are divided over the European Union's next long-term budget, which sets spending priorities and limits from 2028 to 2034. It requires unanimous approval from all 27 member states to pass, as well as a majority vote in favor from members of the European Parliament. Representatives from EU member states met on Wednesday and Thursday to discuss the latest budget proposal from European Council President António Costa, which amounts to a spending plan worth 1.58 trillion euros ($1.73 trillion). It marks a downward revision of around 10% from the original proposals for the bloc's long-term budget — known as the Multiannual Financial Framework, or MFF.

items.title: My self-care ritual is a meal at a fancy restaurant - on my own
items.summary: Solo-dining is being embraced as a self-care trend and it's reshaping the restaurant industry.
items.body: Catherine Smith is perusing the menu at a high-end Mediterranean restaurant she has been excited to try. She has a new outfit on, and as she sips her rosé, she looks across at the empty seat opposite - bliss. "I think what is so special about solo dining is that you don't have to wait for people to make those plans. You can go out and do them yourself," says the 23-year-old. The self-confessed foodie is part of a growing trend of people booking tables for one - not because they're away with work but as a treat. As food trends analyst Charles Banks puts it: "[Eating alone] is becoming an intentional act, a little pocket of independence, indulgence and self-care." We spoke to solo dining fans and hospitality industry experts about how the trend is shaping the restaurant experience and asked if you would book a table for one.

items.summary: Big lenders will aim to ‘protect their earnings’ from temporary increase in corporation tax surcharge, says Andrew Bailey Business live – latest updates The governor of the Bank of England has said he fears banks could attempt to pass on the £1.5bn cost of Labour’s tax increase…
items.body: The governor of the Bank of England has said he fears banks could attempt to pass on the £1.5bn cost of Labour’s tax increase on their profits . The chancellor, John Healey, used his first budget last month to temporarily increase the bank corporation tax surcharge from 3% to 6% for a 15-month period from January, with the proceeds funding “breathing space” to relieve pressure on household finances. While the level of the increase was less than banks had feared – there had been wide speculation that Healey would reinstate the 8% tax level that was in place until 2023 – the Bank’s governor, Andrew Bailey , said he would not be surprised if banks attempted to pass the costs on to customers to “protect their earnings”. “It’s a market economy, so these are decisions banks will have to take,” Bailey said in an interview with the Times.

items.title: The Tech Download: Will Jensen Huang’s return be the spark the shaky AI market needs?
items.summary: AI stocks have fallen in recent times as investors question the sustainability of the AI boom.
items.body: This report is from this week's The Tech Download newsletter. Like what you see? You can subscribe here. The recent Nvidia saga has had more twists and turns than an Agatha Christie novel. It all started with Nvidia co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang 's admission that he had been unfaithful to his wife. Days later, amid an independent board investigation and broader scrutiny over national-security concerns, he resigned. Less than two weeks later, Huang was back at the helm. During all of that, Nvidia stock lost over $1 trillion and then regained just under $1 trillion. The leadership drama has played out at a time when the artificial intelligence market is looking shakier than it has in some time. Neoclouds have seen stocks plummet in recent months as investors question the sustainability of the AI boom. Chip stocks like Arm and AMD have both fallen in the past month.

items.title: Why is there a shortage of 'wizard' elevator mechanics?
items.summary: The pay is good and there's lots of work, so what's behind the shortage of elevator mechanics?
items.body: Some of them are angry. Nerves are frayed. Many of them are just relieved that he's here. When a lift stops working in Chicago, frazzled building managers might get a visit from Jim Lembesis. For more than 47 years, Lembesis has repaired and upgraded lifts. He says he understands why staff and residents are so anxious to have things working again. "They wait and they wait," says Lembesis, a field technician for Parkway Elevators. "There's a lot of frustration. Sometimes it's a repeat issue. It's a never-ending cycle, you know what I mean?" The widely reported shortage of lift and escalator mechanics in the US, which is also a problem in many other countries, has got worse over time, he adds: "It's been like night and day compared to when I started." Everyone needs a lift now and again. Some people depend on them – elderly residents of high-rise buildings, say, or wheelchair users.

items.title: UK’s taste for cow’s milk sours as sales hit record low
items.summary: Environmental and animal welfare concerns, and taste preferences, are behind rising popularity of vegan alternatives Has milk gotta lotta bottle? It may not have as much as it used to, with official data showing Britons are buying less cow’s milk than at any point since records…
items.body: Has milk gotta lotta bottle? It may not have as much as it used to, with official data showing Britons are buying less cow’s milk than at any point since records began. Guardian analysis of the government’s family food survey shows the average person bought 1.8 pints (1,024ml) of cow’s milk a week in 2024-25 – the lowest level in the record’s 52-year history and less than half the amount of milk bought in 1974. So why are people buying less? One reason, say experts, is that the growing accessibility of plant-based milks has created a mindset shift when it comes to dairy – with even meat-eaters changing their habits. “You can get plant-based milk in a lot of different places now and the taste isn’t that different,” says Rosie Green, a professor of environment, food and health at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine.

items.title: Fast cars, big money: Why sportswear races into Formula 1 as sponsorship spending soars 75%
items.summary: Nike, Adidas and Puma are betting big on Formula 1 as the sport's cultural influence grows and younger audiences fuel its appeal.
items.body: The race for dominance in Formula 1 is no longer confined to the racetrack, with some of the world's biggest sportswear brands, including Nike , Adidas and Puma, vying for a piece of the action. Sportswear sponsorship spending in F1 has surged 75% over two years and topped $200 million in 2026, according to Adam Lewis, a senior analyst at research firm Ampere Analysis. Brands are competing for access to the sport's increasingly young and affluent fan base, while looking to capitalize on its growing influence in fashion and popular culture. Nike gave fans a sneak preview of its F1 partnership in Las Vegas this month with a limited-edition collection sold during the Grand Prix. From 2027, Nike will supply F1 staff uniforms, a role Puma has held since 2024, and sell footwear and apparel under the championship's brand. Other sportswear majors have taken a different approach.

items.body: Belgian authorities have ordered Google to halt construction work on a large datacentre in the south of the country because the US tech firm’s requests to modify the original terms of the planning permission did not have approval. “Inspectors visited the site and observed that the building was almost finished, with the structural work completed, even though the permit had been refused,” Raphaël Stokis, a Wallonia regional official, told the public broadcaster RTBF . Stokis said the 300 workers had been given a verbal order to stop work that had been confirmed in writing to Google. The company said in a statement it was “committed to maintaining an open and collaborative dialogue” with the regional authorities. Google’s 2025 application to change its plans, notably including a switch from air to water cooling, was initially approved by local authorities but later revoked after protests.

items.title: Up to 1.4m UK workers risk missing out on zero-hours shake-up, say unions
items.summary: Andy Burnham is warned against calls from bosses to water down employment rights legislation Andy Burnham is being warned that 1.4 million workers will be at risk of being stuck in insecure jobs if a forthcoming ban on zero-hours contracts is watered down. The prime minister is…
items.body: Andy Burnham is being warned that 1.4 million workers will be at risk of being stuck in insecure jobs if a forthcoming ban on zero-hours contracts is watered down. The prime minister is under pressure from business leaders to scale back last year’s Employment Rights Act, which is being introduced in stages over 2026 and 2027. But the leader of the Trades Union Congress, Paul Nowak, said it was “time for the government to deliver” on its manifesto promise. “The business lobby has been pushing to ensure well over a million precarious workers miss out on security at work – that’s not right,” he said. Business leaders are warning that Labour’s plan for the biggest shake-up of employment rights in a generation risks damaging jobs and growth at a perilous moment for the economy.

items.title: Private markets are more accessible than ever for investors. Getting out is another matter
items.summary: Retail access to private markets is growing, but PwC says education lags as redemption limits put liquidity risks in focus.
items.body: Retail investors are lining up to back private funds. But education on how restrictive these funds can be, particularly on when and how much money they can get back, may not be keeping pace with the influx of new capital. PwC research has found that 77% of fund distributors surveyed said access to private markets is becoming important or very important to what they plan to offer clients, but just 15% of asset managers said they provide comprehensive education for retail investors. Unlike the public markets retail investors are more used to, some private-market vehicles limit when investors can get their money back to set repurchase windows, and even then may return only part of what they request.

items.title: The Guardian view on AI and the Riemann hypothesis: a triumph of intelligence, a test of democracy | Editorial
items.summary: Machines are solving problems that have been beyond the reach of human ingenuity. Their growing power must not become the sole preserve of billionaires For the average person, the news that AI has helped crack a problem that has defied mathematicians since 1859 might elicit…
items.body: F or the average person, the news that AI has helped crack a problem that has defied mathematicians since 1859 might elicit momentary awe. What ought to worry everyone is not the discovery per se, but what it says about the power of the machines making it. The pace of scientific discovery looks like it is outrunning the ability of humanity – and its institutions – to understand, let alone regulate, AI’s advances. Last Friday Levent Alpöge , a mathematician at Anthropic, said that he, with the assistance of an unreleased version of the company’s Claude chatbot, had produced what many mathematicians see as the holy grail: a proof for the Riemann hypothesis .

items.title: Sovereign wealth funds are acting more like private equity giants — and inheriting their risks
items.summary: Sovereign wealth funds are increasingly originating deals, taking controlling stakes and building their own investment platforms.
items.body: For decades, sovereign wealth funds were among private equity's most deep-pocketed backers, entrusting billions of dollars to buyout firms to invest on their behalf. Increasingly, they are doing the dealmaking themselves. From originating transactions and taking controlling stakes in companies to building their own investment platforms, some of the world's largest state investors are adopting the playbook of traditional private equity giants, according to industry veterans. "The imminent change is that the lines between LPs and GPs are becoming increasingly blurry. This could bring more fundamental changes in the long term," Diego Lopez of Global SWF told CNBC. Limited partners, or LPs, typically commit capital to private equity funds, while general partners, or GPs, are responsible for sourcing deals and managing investments.

items.title: The food bank helping pet owners with rising bills
items.summary: RSPCA hands out food, vet vouchers, cat litter and toys to pet owners struggling with bills.
items.body: At Burngreave Foodbank in Sheffield, a queue of worried people are here not to collect groceries for themselves, but food for their pets. The RSPCA has launched a pop-up food bank to hand out cat litter, veterinary vouchers and pet toys as well as food. Many of the dog and cat owners using the service say that rising bills are leaving them in fear they will not be able to care for their beloved companions. John Paul Feely, 59, has four cats and a dog, and currently spends £35 a month on them. "At the moment we're facing rises in fuel costs, food costs and you've got to make a choice at some point, can we look after the animals?" he says. Feely worries that unexpected vet bills as well as the day-to-day expenses could tip him over the edge when his energy bill goes up in January.

items.title: Rheinmetall reins in growth ambitions as Europe's rearmament boom hits hurdles
items.summary: The German arms maker vows a "more prudent approch" to forecast sales of tanks and ammunition.
items.body: Rheinmetall is adopting a more "cautious" approach after the German arms maker lost a major contract to build F126 warships for the country's military, in what would have been Rheinmetall's biggest order since World War II. The tank and ammunition maker now expects sales of between 33 and 37 billion euros (between $36.2 billion and $40.6 billion) by 2030, down from a previous forecast of about 45 billion euros, it told investors at its Capital Markets Day on Friday. That guidance incorporates a "more prudent approach" for its large vehicle systems and weapons and ammunition businesses. CEO Armin Papperger said a 2-billion-euro reduction in the 2030 sales target for its vehicle systems business was a strategic decision to build in a "buffer" against potential project delays and supply chain disruptions, rather than a reflection of further lost contracts or weakening demand.

items.summary: Papa John’s order was made without sharing bank security details – tech that could revolutionise shopping Retailers enter the unknown with AI shopping assistants on Black Friday An order of Papa John’s margherita pizzas has become the first purchase in the UK to be made using an…
items.body: An order of Papa John’s margherita pizzas has become the first purchase in the UK to be made using an AI agent using cardless payment technology. The order of nine mini pizzas was made as part of the Financial Conduct Authority’s (FCA) regulated sandbox trials to test the technology, using Lloyds Bank and payment specialist TrueLayer. London-based TrueLayer, which enables payments to be made between bank accounts without using cards, said it was the first time an AI agent had been used to pay a UK retailer for an order for a real customer. “We completed this payment transaction with Papa John’s with no account numbers, no password [and] handled with the highest possible security profile,” said the TrueLayer chief executive, Francesco Simoneschi, in an interview with BBC Radio 4’s Today programme. “We talked with the AI agent, described the occasion and dietary requirements.

items.title: Labour backs bill to stop lawsuits used to silence journalists and whistleblowers
items.summary: Anti-Slapps campaigners criticise draft bill, saying process of dismissing claims will be challenging and costly The government is to back legislation aimed at preventing wealthy and powerful individuals using the courts to silence critics and curb free speech. The justice…
items.body: The government is to back legislation aimed at preventing wealthy and powerful individuals using the courts to silence critics and curb free speech. The justice minister Sarah Sackman told parliament on Friday that Labour would support a private member’s bill sponsored by the Conservative MP John Whittingdale, who is spearheading the latest attempt to bring in anti-Slapp measures in England and Wales. She told the Guardian: “Our legal system should be a route to justice, not a weapon of intimidation, used to evade scrutiny, suppress reporting or discourage people from speaking the truth.” The bill attempts to define abusive cases, often referred to as strategic litigation against public participation, or Slapps, so that they can be dismissed early before defendants incur unaffordable legal costs.

items.title: Trump demands probe into 'record setting error' after third-quarter GDP data gets massive revision higher
items.summary: President Donald Trump on Thursday deemed the latest gross domestic product revision a mistake, claiming that it should be "immediately investigated."
items.body: President Donald Trump on Thursday falsely deemed the latest gross domestic product revision a mistake, claiming that it should be "immediately investigated." Data released Wednesday from the Commerce Department revealed that the U.S. economy exhibited much stronger growth for the third quarter than initially estimated, showing that real GDP grew at a 4.3% annualized rate . That was revised upward from the department's advance estimate of 3.4%. That revision was a "RECORD SETTING ERROR," Trump said in a Truth Social post , suggesting that the initial release could have influenced the outcome of the 2026 U.S. midterm elections , where Democrats flipped both chambers of Congress and multiple governorships.

items.title: Water firms to identify 250,000 vulnerable households in England eligible for discounts
items.summary: Department for Work and Pensions to provide data about households missing out on WaterSure support scheme Water companies will use government data to identify as many as 250,000 vulnerable households in England eligible for discounts, after criticism that not enough people are…
items.body: Water companies will use government data to identify as many as 250,000 vulnerable households in England eligible for discounts, after criticism that not enough people are aware of the £428 support for their annual bills. The Department for Work and Pensions will provide information to identify and contact a quarter of a million households who are missing out on support to which they are entitled under the WaterSure scheme . The scheme is open to people on benefits who need to use a lot of water either for medical reasons or because their household has three or more children under 19. The government said that 300,000 customers are signed up to WaterSure , but fewer than half of eligible households claim it because either they are unaware or they may have difficulty proving they qualify. The Labour government has sought to portray itself as tough on the water industry.

items.title: Too old for soft toys? Tell that to kidults booking up the Harrods Jellycat cafe
items.summary: Department stores are hosting in-person events for those who find comfort in collecting the British soft toy brand They’re cute, cuddly and taking over the homes of young adults. Jellycat, a British soft toy brand founded in 1999, is experiencing a rise in interest from adult…
items.body: Jellycat, a British soft toy brand founded in 1999, is experiencing a rise in interest from adult buyers as they snap up signature smiley designs in the shape of everything from croissants and disco balls to turtles and teabags. The trend is part of a wider “kidult” movement, with grownups buying items traditionally geared towards children, for example, Lego sets and Pokémon cards . On social media, videos of users talking through their collections of soft toys known as plushies can rack up millions of views. On Monday, Harrods in London is opening “a first-of-its-kind dining destination” – a Jellycat cafe serving brunch in edible and soft toy form. Diners will be able to buy a peach granola bowl-shaped plushie, and eat the dish too. According to research by Circana, “kidult” toy sales in the UK grew 22% in the first half of 2026.

items.title: Australian LNG exporters must reserve some supply to lower domestic prices
items.body: CANBERRA -- Australian liquefied natural gas exporters will be required to direct the equivalent of 20% of their exports to the country's domestic market, starting in 2028, under a new law passed by Parliament that has been welcomed by manufacturers but slammed by the LNG industry. The legislation, approved on Friday, aims to reduce prices by creating an oversupply of 10% above forecast demand for the domestic market. Exporters can seek permission to reduce their 20% obligation if necessary to meet an existing export contract, or because of infrastructure constraints.
